Question 1 of 10: What did "keep doing what you're doing" mean?

I heard it as praise. In the room, it was a plan.

A sentence with no verb of change in it is a sentence about staying. The plan for you has already been written, and that's it. Same family: "you're on the radar," "we want to set you up for success," "let's revisit next cycle."

I said some of these as a leader before I understood what they were doing. None of them is said with bad intent. That's what makes them hard to catch. Every one sounds like development and keeps you exactly where you're useful.

The script: "For how long? If I do exactly this for another year, what changes?"

You'll leave with a date, or with the knowledge that there isn't one. Both are information.

Question 2 of 10: Okay, but what do I say back?

This was the number one reply when I decoded corporate praise. Knowing what "you're the glue" means is half of it. The other half is the next sentence out of your mouth.

The move in every one is the same: take the warm, vague version and ask for specifics, on a date, in writing.

"You're such a team player." Say back: "I'm glad it helps. What I want next is to own [specific area]. Can we map how I get there?"

"You're the glue that holds this team together." Say back: "Then let's make it official. If this falls apart without me, that's a role, not a favor. Can we write it up as owned scope?"

"We really value your work here." Say back: "I'm glad. I want that to show up as a level and a title. What's the path, and who else needs to be convinced?"

None of those is a confrontation. Each one asks a warm sentence to get specific.

Question 3 of 10: Who is my sponsor, and do they have any pull?

Praise is free. Someone can champion you warmly in every conversation you're present for and never once have spent anything on you.

I was sure I had a sponsor on GPS III. Four promotion cycles went by. I had a supporter.

Three tests. They take ten minutes and you can run them tonight on names you already know.

Has this person ever spent something on you? Look for a stretch assignment or your name attached to something visible that you weren't chasing.

Can they say yes on their own? Someone who has to go and ask on your behalf is a supporter. Worth having. It won't move you.

Who else have they moved? If nobody in their orbit has been promoted, they may be well meaning and powerless.

Run all three and you land on one of two answers: you've been investing in someone who can't help you, or you already have a real sponsor and have been too polite to ask them for anything.

Question 4 of 10: How do I reach out to a senior leader when I don't have a specific topic?

Two questions do the job a topic would, and only they can answer them.

The first goes to your own manager, in your next 1:1: "From where you sit, who are the leaders you think I should be building stronger connections with?" You walk out with names, and your manager walks out knowing you're building toward something.

The second goes to the senior person other people quote. Katie Liljenquist tested this. Sellers in a negotiation who pushed hard closed 8% of the time. Sellers who asked the buyer for advice closed 42%. Asking for advice makes someone the expert in the room, and once they've played that role for you, they stay invested in seeing you use it.

So bring something unfinished. "You've run more of these than I have. This is the call I'm leaning toward, and why. What would you change?"

If it's someone you worked with years ago, the first message carries information instead of a request: "I saw your team's launch went out last week. You ran the integration side when we worked together, so I knew what that took. I wanted you to know where I landed."

The sign it landed: they come back to you unprompted.

Who's the senior person you've been drafting a message to for a month?

Question 5 of 10: I'm doing the next-level job without the title. How do I get the title?

They handed me the job and kept the title. I was the spacecraft bus chief engineer, then they handed me the flight operations manual for the entire spacecraft, a level up. I ran it for two years. Review came. The title didn't. "You're next. Let's revisit at midyear."

Years later I sat in those rooms. We never measured a woman against her gaps. We started from a short list of names and argued about the people already on it.

A title is a decision made against a slate. Doing the job proves you can do the job. It doesn't put you on the slate.

Three questions for your next 1:1. "When something opens at that level, is there a list of people who get considered, and am I on it?" "Is this the reason I wasn't moved, or is it development advice?" "Besides you, who would have to be comfortable with this?"

Then get the delegation said out loud. Write one page: the scope you own today, the decisions you make without asking, the people who come to you. Bring it to your manager and ask: "Is this the scope you intended me to hold?" Once it's on paper, it's a role. Until then, it's a favor you're doing.

Have you ever been told you were next, and then watched a midyear come and go?

Question 6 of 10: Someone else briefed my work. What do I do about it?

I've watched this one stall the careers of 100+ women. The idea leaves her mouth and comes back wearing someone else's name, and she spends the next week deciding whether saying something would make her look petty.

It's an attribution gap in the system, and paper closes it faster than a confrontation ever will.

When you float the idea, attach the owner in the same breath: "The outcome we're driving is X, and I'll own the model for it."

When the room moves on, send the recap yourself, same day: "Capturing what we agreed on: [your idea]. I'll take the next step on the model." Silence makes credit available. Notes make it permanent.

When someone repeats it and the room loves it, reconnect calmly, with a detail only the author would have: "Glad this landed. When I built the first version, the risk I designed around was X. Happy to share the background."

Then keep a ledger. Date, the idea, where you said it, who was in the room, the follow-up you sent. Ten minutes every Friday.

What's the line you use when your idea comes back in someone else's voice?

Question 7 of 10: I can't put a number on what I did. How do I prove it?

I said that sentence for years. I've also read the other side of those reviews, and it costs more than a weak quarter ever did.

We hand in adjectives. Strong contributor. Great partner. Invaluable. Adjectives get read out loud and set down. A number gets written on the sheet.

Almost every significant thing you've done fits one of six categories: risk retired, revenue enabled, cost lowered, time recovered, quality raised, relationship saved. If a win can't be measured, you haven't found its category yet.

The formula: what I did, plus what it prevented or enabled, plus the number. "I ran the design reviews" becomes "I led my team through 43 preliminary and 43 critical design reviews, both rounds 6 months ahead of schedule."

When the clean figure doesn't exist, estimate it and say so. An honest estimate is still a number, and a number is something a decision maker can defend when you aren't there.

Which category holds your biggest uncounted win?

Question 8 of 10: Is it me, or am I reading into things?

Harvard Business Review has asked executives the same questions since 1965. They asked whether women are judged more harshly than men. Twenty years ago, 35% of men and 35% of women said yes. Today the men still say 35%. The women say 90%.

The men are describing the workplace they think exists. The women are describing the one they live in.

So the answer to "is it me" is usually no, and a feeling won't win that argument. A record will.

Keep a Pattern Log. One line per incident, four fields, thirty seconds: what happened in one neutral sentence, the date and who was in the room, what it cost, and whether it's happened before.

Then don't touch it for a quarter. When you read ninety days at once, you stop asking "did that really happen?" and start seeing what repeats.

And the next time the word with no metric comes up, say back: "Which results, which rooms, and which people need to see this before next cycle?" If no one can answer, the word was describing the room's comfort, and you can stop auditing yourself for it.

Question 9 of 10: Two review cycles, nothing changed. When is it time to force a date?

Now. Two cycles with the same words is the signal.

Lay your last two reviews side by side and mark every development item that repeats word for word. A live case gets gaps marked closed and new ones named. When the same words come back a second year, the review is holding you where you are.

Then ask for the role and the date, in your next 1:1: "What specific role am I being developed toward, and when does it get discussed next?" A live case comes back with a role name and a month. A quality instead, like "more executive presence," means you're being described rather than planned for.

Same day, put it in writing: "To make sure I heard it right, can you confirm the role and the timing we talked about?"

A live case gets a reply that repeats the role and the date. A closed one gets silence, or the adjectives again.

Which of your development items has shown up two years running?

Question 10 of 10: Should I just leave?

Sometimes. I'll say that out loud, because most career advice won't.

If you ran the three tests from last night and got two closed answers, effort has stopped being the variable, and more of it won't change the outcome. Start building your case somewhere it can still be argued: another team, or another company.

Will Larson surveyed the engineers who made it past the level most companies expect you to stay at. About a third had to change companies to get the title. Getting past that grade is a separate budget decision, and it isn't made on your timeline.

Before you decide, ask one question about where you are: "Who got past that level from inside in the last five years?" One name is enough. If everyone above the line was hired in, the internal path is a drawing, and now you know it.

Your record goes with you. The room closed the case. You didn't.

If your case is closed where you are, where would you take it?

I spent 6 weeks proving myself to the wrong room.

Six weeks in Kazakhstan, in the dead of winter, at the Baikonur Cosmodrome. I was deputy program manager in a stretch role, leading closeout on a communications satellite that was the first commercial payload on a Russian Proton in that configuration.

Three years better at the job. Seven years behind on pay.

Wharton's Matthew Bidwell studied it: outside hires take three years to perform as well as internal hires in the same job, and internal hires take seven years to earn as much as outside hires are paid.

I wrote the compensation plans for a 450-person engineering org. Your raise and a stranger's offer get set by two different comparisons. Yours runs against the people already here. Theirs runs against what it costs to get somebody to say yes.

"We want to be fair across the team." I was told that. It's true, inside one comparison. The team is the people who also stayed.

Take the recruiter call you've been declining. Twenty minutes: "I'm not looking. I'll give you twenty minutes if you'll tell me what this role pays." Then ask your manager what triggers an out-of-cycle adjustment.

Which call are you making first?
